title: Maker's Schedule, Manager's Schedule
candidate_workflows: Classify work as maker or manager work before scheduling it; preserve half-day maker blocks and evaluate meetings by their interruption cost, not merely their duration.
Cluster meetings into office-hour blocks at the end of a work period, or explicitly partition maker and business work into separate uninterrupted shifts.

title: Ramen Profitable
candidate_workflows: Gate ramen profitability on the product's capital needs: calculate the founder-living-cost threshold only when a capital-light startup can plausibly reach it, and use a different runway plan for capital-heavy categories.

When applicable, pursue non-harmful interim revenue sufficient for survival without requiring launch-day charging or treating that revenue source as the final business model; once crossed, use the optionality to bound fundraising and protect product attention.
Allow limited service work as a bridge, but regularly verify that it is producing a repeatable product rather than turning the company into a consultancy.

title: The Trouble with the Segway
candidate_workflows: Test not only functional utility but how target users feel and look while using the product in its real social setting.

Grow through sellable iterations exposed to real users; treat focus groups and secret development as insufficient substitutes for unfiltered public behavior, especially after an easy fundraise reduces pressure to learn.

title: What Kate Saw in Silicon Valley
candidate_workflows: Treat the initial idea as provisional: launch quickly, listen to users, and follow evidence into a materially different product when necessary.
Prepare founders for continual failure risk and emotional volatility, then build resilience through scrappy execution, experienced advice, and peer help.
Protect long stretches of solitary production time while deliberately using the local founder network for feedback and assistance.

title: The Anatomy of Determination
candidate_workflows: Evaluate founders for sustained determination rather than confusing intelligence or talent with the ability to keep a startup moving.

Diagnose determination as willfulness balanced by discipline and aimed by ambition; strengthen the cultivable parts through explicit self-constraints, progressively harder achievements, and ambitious peers.
Direct persistence toward other people's needs and revisit the destination so energy does not harden into inert stubbornness or an attractive local maximum.

title: The List of N Things
candidate_workflows: Use a numbered list when the material is genuinely a set of independent items, when readers need random access, or when a fast low-resolution draft is more valuable than a continuous argument.
Draft the complete scaffold first and raise its resolution incrementally, but do not imply exhaustiveness unless the catalog is actually complete.
Avoid a fixed list when the purpose is discovery, because predetermined compartments constrain the new ideas that can emerge while writing.

title: Post-Medium Publishing
candidate_workflows: Separate the value customers receive from the physical medium or controlled channel that historically enabled charging, then test whether buyers pay because the information creates money, is necessary software, or is merely convenient to access.
When a distribution medium collapses, choose explicitly between free distribution with indirect revenue and embodying the information in a paid product or experience.
Favor opportunities where new technology gives users something previously unavailable; treat attempts to preserve an obsolete revenue source without new user value as a warning sign.

title: Persuade xor Discover
candidate_workflows: Choose whether a document is meant to discover truth or persuade a specific audience before drafting; do not silently optimize for both.

For discovery work, remove audience-pleasing padding and compress the claim until its logical parts are visible, then protect faint or surprising observations from anticipated objections until they are understood.
For persuasion work, identify any framing added for acceptance and verify that it does not alter the underlying claim or hide contrary evidence from the writer.

title: What Startups Are Really Like
candidate_workflows: Choose cofounders for character, commitment, and tested working relationships, then maintain the relationship as deliberately as the product.
Plan for a multiyear emotional and operational grind: set expectations that progress is incremental, preserve morale, and avoid making one feature, deal, or outside party the single path to survival.

Cross-source safety gate from article 153: when exposure is reversible and error costs are low, ship the smallest complete product with a quantum of utility, start a user conversation, and change the hypothesis as evidence warrants; when mistakes can cause serious harm or irreversible loss, require risk-appropriate validation before exposure. Attentive service can offset incompleteness, not unsafe or incorrect behavior.

When adoption stalls, distinguish insufficient exposure from a weak product and from switching or integration friction; choose product improvement and word of mouth when technical quality can drive distribution, or deals and marketing when the product type requires them.
Keep slow investors, large customers, and deals off the critical path; assume uncommitted money will not arrive and fork external processes from product progress.

Treat investor preference for displayed certainty and social proof as a selection-pressure observation, not advice to deceive. Cross-source resolution from article 154: respond with truth-first evidence, domain command, candor about rejection and risk, and a concise explanation investors can retell rather than feigned certainty.

Model outcomes as skill multiplied by determination and luck: improve the controllable inputs, evaluate founders and decisions using information available beforehand, and do not treat success or failure alone as proof of their quality.
Revisit the technical founder's job every six to twelve months and deliberately shift from coding toward hiring, planning, management, and the next stage's constraints as the company grows.

title: Apple's Mistake
candidate_workflows: Design software release policy around frequent small changes and rapid bug fixes; measure every gate by how it affects iteration speed and the quality users actually receive.
Treat platform developers as both users and distribution partners, monitor trust as an operating metric, and correct policies that make strong builders reluctant to join or invest in the ecosystem.
When searching for product opportunities, notice personal projects built by founders for themselves and unmet needs that a dominant platform's restrictions make impossible to serve.

title: Organic Startup Ideas
candidate_workflows: Inventory what is missing or broken in the founders' daily lives, especially around newly available technology, and build the fix the founders themselves want.
Treat a useful personal project as an experiment before forcing it to look like a company; follow repeated use and adjacent demand even when outsiders dismiss the first version as a toy.
If the idea targets unfamiliar users, become one of them or reproduce their workflow closely enough to replace prediction from afar with direct experience.

title: How to Lose Time and Money
candidate_workflows: Build explicit review alarms for decisions that resemble responsible investment but can destroy capital, rather than relying only on instincts against obvious consumption.
At the end of a work period, name the concrete output produced and reclassify desk-bound activity such as email as busywork when it repeatedly yields none.
Compare hidden traps with the overtly indulgent behavior they replace so virtue-signaling form does not exempt an activity from an outcome check.

title: The Top Idea in Your Mind
candidate_workflows: Audit the team's top idea by observing what thoughts recur during unstructured moments, not by naming what everyone wishes they were thinking about.
If fundraising, acquisition talk, money, or a dispute has displaced product thinking, change the underlying dependency or situation instead of trying to suppress the thought directly.
Choose conditions where the most urgent recurring problem is one the company wants solved, and keep unavoidable fundraising bounded to a deliberate short interval.

title: The Acceleration of Addictiveness
candidate_workflows: Assume tools and media can become more attention-capturing after adoption, and periodically re-audit existing habits instead of evaluating only new products.
Do not use statistical normality as evidence that a habit supports good work when social defenses lag technological change.
Create personal boundaries before a shared custom exists, such as device limits or long offline periods, and judge them by whether they restore uninterrupted thought and production.

title: The Future of Startup Funding
candidate_workflows: Match investor quality and round structure to the startup's capital need and stage, but treat the essay's super-angel, rolling-close, standardized-document, and varying-note-cap mechanics as a 2010 market forecast rather than timeless instrument instructions.

For capital-light software startups, seek independent commitments in a bounded process; if a rolling close fits the current round, use it to reduce coordination deadlock and finish sooner, never to make fundraising continuous.
Reject contingencies and tranches that create deadlock or one-sided options, inspect option-pool dilution, and compare investors by their willingness to decide independently.
Set a fast close target and keep fundraising out of the product's critical path, because delay transfers leverage to investors and displaces company-building attention.
Reassess founder control against the funding cycle: seller's markets can increase leverage, while a downturn can reduce it without invalidating the durable need for speed and bounded attention.

title: What Happened to Yahoo
candidate_workflows: Audit whether lucrative revenue is aligned with user value or masking a better product direction; compare what skilled internal users choose with what current customers overpay for.

State whether software is strategically central even when the company monetizes through another model, then give technical builders product reasoning and ownership rather than treating programming as translation work.
Protect talent density through unusually selective technical hiring and a culture where strong programmers work with peers they respect; treat declining builder quality as a compounding risk.

title: High Resolution Fundraising
candidate_workflows: Break investor waiting games by offering earlier or more helpful investors better effective terms in exchange for real commitment or value.
Use lightweight standardized notes or equity documents that permit different prices without renegotiating the whole round.
Start with a smaller target and expand when demand is strong, or close a smaller round when demand is weak, instead of selecting a fixed amount before observing investors.

title: Where to See Silicon Valley
candidate_workflows: For an early startup, compare office locations by whether people willingly remain there beyond formal hours; favor walkable access to food and public activity that supports shared meals, informal idea discussion, and returning to implement together.

title: The New Funding Landscape
candidate_workflows: Map each investor type by check size, decision speed, attention, follow-on motive, and board expectations before choosing a round structure.
Compare a larger VC round with a medium angel round on dilution, founder control, time to close, and whether a rejection leaves the company with nothing or a smaller completed round.
Collect the most committed checks first, update price or round size as demand becomes visible, and treat the process as incremental feedback rather than a single final vote.
Mitigate signalling risk by limiting dependence on any one VC and prioritizing measurable revenue or usage before the next round so company results dominate investor inference.
